title: Attention
hook: what we look at shapes us: Paul's list of things to think on (Philippians 4:8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke the beloved physician, and a Samaritan with oil and wine. Your line was God heals through hands. Whose hands did you thank, and what did you tell them? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.

Quick question, no wrong answers: what was the last thing you looked at before this lesson started? And the thing before that? And before that? For some of us the trail runs back through a string of small screens, each a few seconds long, none of them chosen exactly. Paul, writing to the church at Philippi while he's in chains, closes his letter with a list. It isn't a list of rules. It's a list of things to look at, and keep looking at, until they shape you. Today: attention.

Here's the list, in the King James Bible: "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things." Notice what kind of list it is. Not a list of things to avoid. A list of things to go looking for. The words think on translate a Greek word for reckoning, the kind of counting a bookkeeper does. Take account of these. Add them up. Let them be what you keep track of. Jesus says something close in the Sermon on the Mount: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light." In Jesus' picture, what you look at doesn't stay outside you. It gets in. It becomes the light you live by. And because that's hard, the Psalms turn it into a request: "Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity." Guarding your gaze, in this tradition, isn't only willpower. It's something asked for. So Christians who take this seriously do two things at once. They turn away from some things, not out of fear, but because a gaze is limited and the hours are few. And they turn toward something better: a face across the table, a page worth reading, a sky, a true word. Attention is something you give. Paul's question is what you're giving it to.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE BODY IS THE EYE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one real thing, slowly. Put your phone face down, out of reach if you can. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing in front of you: a window, your own hands, a plant, a cup. Look at it as if you'd been asked to describe it to someone who can't see. Its color. Its edges. Where the light lands. When the pull to check something comes, and it may, notice it, and come back. If you pray, you can use the line from the Psalms: "Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity." The bell holds the time.
Attention. Where you point your eyes and mind: Paul says think on what is true and lovely, and Jesus calls the eye the light of the body.

Your line: guard your gaze. Today, take one hour off screens, and spend part of it on one thing from Paul's list: something true, something lovely, something worth praise. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians practice this through daily scripture reading, times of silence, fasting from media during seasons like Lent, and examining at day's end what they gave their attention to.

fork.setup: you're Paul, in chains, closing a letter to a church you love. they live in a busy city full of distractions. what do you leave them with?
options: a list of everything they must stop looking at.
a list of good things to look for and think on.
nothing; what they look at is their own business.
fork.reveal: Paul writes a list of things to seek: "whatsoever things are true... think on these things." he steers attention toward the good instead of only away from the bad.

original.note: Greek: reckon, take account of; the word behind "think on these things" in Philippians 4:8.

trapdoor: what you thought: try not to look at bad things.
what it means: go looking for what is true, honest, just, pure and lovely, and keep looking, because what you look at shapes you.
what a scholar hears: "think on" renders logizesthe, a word for reckoning or counting up, as in keeping accounts: keep track of these.
